parts.title: Using Tiny Liquid Jets and Light to Measure How the Light-Sensing Part of a Yellow Protein Holds On to Its Electrons in Water
parts.abstract:
Photoactive yellow protein (PYP) is a well-known example of a light sensor. In the bacterium Halorhodospira halophila, it helps the cell sense harmful ultraviolet (UV) light and move away from it. When PYP is dissolved in water, it is known to react with oxygen after absorbing light, a process called photooxidation. At the heart of PYP sits a small molecule called the chromophore, the part that actually captures the light. In water, this chromophore loses a hydrogen ion and becomes negatively charged. Until now, no one had measured two things about this charged chromophore in water. The first is its vertical detachment energy: the energy needed to knock an electron straight out of the molecule without letting the molecule change shape first. The second is its electronic structure, meaning how its electrons are arranged.

To find out, we used a method called liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy. In this method, a very thin jet of liquid flows through a vacuum, and we shine light on it. The light knocks electrons out of the molecules, and we measure how tightly those electrons were held. We used three kinds of light: X-rays, extreme ultraviolet (EUV) light, and ultraviolet (UV) light. For the UV light, we used several photons at once, because each UV photon carries too little energy on its own. We backed up our measurements with detailed computer calculations of the molecule's electrons.

We found two ways of measuring the energy needed to remove an electron. The vertical detachment energy was 6.8 ± 0.1 eV. The adiabatic detachment energy, which allows the molecule to relax into its most comfortable shape after the electron leaves, was around 5.9 eV. (An electronvolt, eV, is a tiny unit of energy used for atoms and molecules.)

Our UV measurements confirmed a high-energy "resonance" close to the point where electrons start to escape. A resonance is an energy level that the molecule can easily reach, and it makes the molecule respond much more strongly. This resonance needs two photons to reach, and it could be responsible for the photooxidation caused by UV light. The measurements also revealed a three-photon resonance in the detachment continuum, the range of energies above which electrons can escape freely.

This work shows how powerful it is to combine X-ray, EUV and UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy. Together, they can reveal the electronic structure of light-capturing molecules that dissolve only weakly in water. This opens the way to a deeper understanding of the part these molecules play in how living things use light.
parts.introduction_first:
Photoactive proteins are found everywhere in living things, and they often control how a living organism responds to the light around it. Photoactive yellow protein (PYP) is the light sensor that makes the bacterium Halorhodospira halophila move away from light. Scientists have studied it a great deal as a typical example of a light sensor.

At the heart of PYP is its chromophore, the small molecule that captures the light. This chromophore is a molecule called trans-p-coumaric acid that has lost a hydrogen ion, so it carries a negative charge. It is attached to one of the protein's building blocks, a cysteine, through a chemical link called a thioester. A network of hydrogen bonds, weak attractions between molecules, holds it in place.

Researchers have studied the photocycle of PYP, the chain of changes it goes through after absorbing light. They have used several methods. These include X-ray crystallography, which uses X-rays to see the shape of molecules, and optical transient absorption, which tracks how the molecule absorbs light over very short times. They also include infrared spectroscopy, which uses infrared light to learn about the molecule's bonds.

The photocycle begins when the chromophore absorbs a photon of blue light. It absorbs most strongly at a wavelength of 446 nm, which corresponds to an energy of 2.78 eV. This light makes a double bond in the chromophore, a C=C bond, switch from a straight "trans" shape to a bent "cis" shape. That switch sets off a cascade of changes in the protein's structure, which signals that harmful UV light is present.

To fully understand this shape-changing step, we need a clear picture of the chromophore's electronic structure. We also need to know how the complicated surroundings inside the protein can adjust the way the chromophore responds to light.
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

We used X-ray and EUV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy to measure the first two vertical detachment energies of pCE–. This is a model version of the light-capturing part of yellow protein. Its vertical detachment energies were 6.8 ± 0.1 eV and 7.8 ± 0.1 eV. These values agree excellently with our computer calculations, which gave 6.7 and 7.8 eV. We used a calculation method called XMCQDPT2/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP. We also used the points where the X-ray, EUV and UV spectra begin to rise. From these, we estimated the first adiabatic detachment energy of pCE–, which is about 5.9 eV.

Next, we used UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy to follow the routes by which pCE– loses an electron after it is excited to its first excited state, S1. We did this across wavelengths from 410 to 310 nm. We changed the laser power to tell apart routes that use one photon from routes that use two. We also changed the wavelength to separate two different two-photon routes that start from S1.

The first route is direct. It goes through a high-energy excited state that lies close to the point where electrons can escape freely. Earlier work had suggested that this state helps form solvated electrons, which are electrons that have broken free and are surrounded by water molecules. We inferred this high-energy resonance from two clues. The first was the difference between the one-photon and two-photon electron binding energies of S1. The second was a change in the slope of the two-photon electrons' kinetic energy as the photon energy changed.

The second route is autodetachment. Here, the electron escapes from a high-energy excited state that sits inside the range of energies where electrons can escape freely. Resonances like this are often seen in isolated negatively charged molecules in the gas phase that hold on to their electrons only weakly. Our work provides experimental evidence that similar low-energy resonances exist just above the escape point for negatively charged molecules dissolved in water.
parts.introduction_rest:
Earlier studies looked at the isolated PYP chromophore in the gas phase, as a negatively charged molecule. They changed the chromophore's chemistry and shape on purpose and watched how this affected its electronic structure and the way it behaves after absorbing light. One part of the chromophore stood out. It is the carbonyl tail, a C=O group at one end of the molecule, and the groups of atoms attached to it. These groups turned out to play a role in how the electrons are arranged and in how the molecule moves through its excited states.

Chromophores with stronger electron-accepting groups had higher vertical detachment energies. An electron-accepting group pulls electrons toward itself. The stronger it pulls, the more it holds the electron in place, so more energy is needed to remove it. Other studies used "locks" around the double bond or around the single bond next to it. These locks stop the molecule from turning around those bonds. They showed that two kinds of turning guide the molecule toward conical intersections with its ground state, the molecule's most stable, lowest-energy form. A conical intersection is a point where two energy levels meet, so the molecule can switch from one to the other. Here, the molecule switches from an excited state to the ground state.

Similar observations came from time-resolved experiments on model versions of the PYP chromophore dissolved in water. These experiments follow how a molecule changes over very short times. They showed that the electron-accepting strength of the group attached to the carbonyl tail affects how fast the chromophore relaxes, meaning how quickly it settles into a new shape. The same group also decides whether the chromophore switches from the trans shape to the cis shape. Chromophores with strong electron acceptors relax quickly. They pass through a short-lived in-between form, in which the phenolate part of the molecule is twisted, and end up in the trans shape. Chromophores with weak electron acceptors relax more slowly and go straight to the cis shape.

Transient absorption spectroscopy studies have also shown that solvated electrons form when PYP and its chromophore absorb light in water. These studies proposed that the solvated electrons formed through a two-photon process. In this process, two photons together give the electron enough energy to escape. The clue was that the signal from the solvated electrons grew with the square of the laser pulse energy. In other words, doubling the pulse energy made the signal four times stronger.

However, how the solvated electrons form is still debated. There are two main ideas. In the first, the electron moves into a charge-transfer-to-solvent state, in which the electron has already passed into the surrounding water. In the second, the electron passes through a short-lived in-between state that is reached by one photon and then a second photon. For PYP in water, the solvated electron drifts away from the chromophore, and this drifting controls how quickly the two recombine. The electron and the chromophore, which has become a radical, are a pair that started out together. The rate at which they recombine gave a diffusion coefficient, a number that describes how fast something spreads out by drifting. This value was similar to that of electrons in water.

So measuring the detachment energies, and studying the higher-energy excited states thought to help form solvated electrons in water, can tell us about the photoredox properties of this important chromophore. These are the ways it takes part in light-driven chemical reactions that move electrons around. That knowledge can then serve as a basis for understanding similar processes in living things.

Liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy is one of the most powerful ways to study the electronic structure of molecules dissolved in water. It directly measures electron binding energies, which are the energies that hold electrons in a molecule. X-ray and EUV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy are excellent for measuring accurate electron binding energies of dissolved molecules in their ground state. Their photons carry so much energy that the knocked-out electrons have kinetic energies of about 15 eV or more. Kinetic energy is the energy of motion. Electrons that lose some energy on the way out, called inelastically scattered electrons, then have much lower energies. This keeps them well apart from the features we want to measure.

X-ray and EUV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy have a challenge with organic chromophores that dissolve only weakly. Water itself gives off a huge number of electrons, because water is so plentiful. To get a clear signal from the chromophore, researchers generally need a high concentration of the dissolved molecule, about 5 mM or more, or they need to collect data for a long time.

UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy has an advantage. It can use several photons at once to knock electrons out of molecules at concentrations measured in μM, which is a thousand times lower than mM. This works because UV photons do not carry enough energy on their own to knock electrons out of water. At these low concentrations, and with only a little added salt, the molecules are less likely to clump together or to react with water, for example by hydrolysis, which means being broken apart by water.

UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy can also use a resonance to boost the signal. This lets it measure electron binding energies of excited states. These energies decide how processes such as charge transfer unfold, and other methods can struggle to measure them. One challenge with UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy has been that most of the energy lost by electrons on the way out is small, less than 1 eV. This distorts the spectra. However, recent progress in recovering the true photoelectron spectra from these distorted ones has made UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy a powerful tool for working out the electronic structure of organic chromophores that dissolve only weakly.

In this paper, we combine X-ray, EUV and UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy, with the UV light used in several photons at once. We study the negatively charged methyl ester version of trans-p-coumaric acid, called pCE– (Figure). We work in water to find the vertical detachment energies and to estimate the adiabatic detachment energies. We also explore the higher-energy excited states. To help us interpret our measurements, we use computer calculations of two kinds. The first is multistep molecular dynamics, which follows how the atoms move over time. The second is quantum mechanics/effective-fragment potential, which calculates the electrons while treating the surrounding water in a simplified way.
parts.methods:
Methods

### Experiments

We made water solutions of pCE–, the negatively charged form of the chromophore. To do this, we used pCE (more than 98.0% pure, from Tokyo Chemical Industries) and sodium hydroxide, NaOH (from Sigma-Aldrich). We then sonicated the solutions for up to 2 hours. Sonication means shaking the liquid with sound waves, and we kept going until the pCE– had fully dissolved.

For the X-ray and EUV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy measurements, we also added a salt to each solution so that it could carry enough electricity. We added sodium fluoride (NaF) for the X-ray measurements and sodium chloride (NaCl) for the EUV measurements.

We also measured how strongly pCE absorbs UV and visible light. We used a UV-2600i spectrophotometer (made by Shimadzu), an instrument that measures how much light of each colour a sample absorbs. We recorded these steady-state absorption spectra for 50 μM pCE in 2.0 mM water containing NaOH. (μM and mM are units of concentration: μM means millionths of a mole per litre, and mM means thousandths of a mole per litre.)

For the X-ray measurements, we used a solution of 5.0 mM pCE in water with 5.5 mM NaOH and 30 mM NaF. We recorded the X-ray photoelectron spectra at the U49/2 PGM-1 beamline of the BESSY II synchrotron in Berlin. A beamline is the station where the X-ray light is produced and used. The X-ray beam there has a focal size of 20 × 80 μm². We used a photoelectron spectrometer described in detail elsewhere. It has two parts. One is an interaction chamber, where the liquid jet meets the X-rays. The other is a hemispherical electron analyzer, a curved, half-sphere-shaped detector that sorts electrons by their energy. The two parts are connected by a differentially pumped tube, which keeps the pressure low in the analyzer without letting the chamber fill with gas.

We cooled the solutions to 12 °C. We then fed them into the interaction chamber through a fused silica nozzle 25 μm wide, at a speed of about 20 m per second. We did not apply any voltage to the liquid jet. Instead, we connected it to the spectrometer's ground. The X-ray energy was 180 eV. The energy resolution of the experiment, meaning the smallest energy difference we could tell apart, was less than 125 meV. (A meV, or millielectronvolt, is one thousandth of an eV.) This limit came from the energy resolution of the detection system (about 100 meV) and of the beamline (about 100 meV).

For the EUV measurements, we used a helium discharge source (Scienta Omicron VUV5K). It produced a single, pure line of light called He II α, with an energy of 40.81 eV. We ran these experiments on the EASI setup (Electronic structure of Aqueous Solutions and Interfaces). It also has a hemispherical electron analyzer and an interaction chamber that holds the liquid microjet.

We used two solutions. The first contained 5.0 mM pCE in water with 5.5 mM NaOH and 50 mM NaCl. The second contained only 50 mM NaCl. We kept both at 20 °C. We applied a voltage of −25 V to the solutions before feeding them into the chamber. A high-performance liquid chromatography pump pushed them through a fused silica nozzle 26 μm wide, at a flow rate of 1.5 mL per minute. We kept the pressure in the interaction region between 1 × 10⁻⁴ and 4 × 10⁻⁴ mbar. (A mbar is a unit of pressure, and these values are far below normal air pressure.) The light from the helium source, with its energy spread narrowed to about 1 meV (measured as the full width at half maximum), crossed the liquid jet. The hemispherical analyzer then detected the photoelectrons in energy bins 25 meV wide.

For the UV measurements, we used a liquid-microjet magnetic-bottle time-of-flight (TOF) photoelectron spectrometer, described in detail elsewhere. In this instrument, a magnetic field guides the electrons along a long tube. We then record how long each electron takes to travel the tube, which tells us how fast it was moving.

We fed water solutions of 5 or 50 μM pCE in 1.0–3.5 mM NaOH through a fused silica nozzle 20 μm wide. A high-performance liquid chromatography pump pushed them through at flow rates between 0.50 and 0.95 mL per minute. We changed the NaOH concentration and the flow rate of the jet for one reason. Inside the nozzle, the liquid picks up an electric charge as it flows, an effect called electrokinetic charging. This charge changes the vacuum level, the energy that electrons need to escape, at the walls of the interaction region compared with the vacuum level at the jet. We adjusted the two settings to keep this difference as small as possible.

We crossed the liquid jet with tunable femtosecond laser pulses (410–310 nm, 4–10 nJ per pulse) about 1 mm below the nozzle opening. A femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a second. The liquid then flowed into a cold trap. We detected the photoelectrons at the end of the TOF tube, recording their arrival time relative to the moment the laser pulse was triggered.

We also recorded photoelectron spectra of nitric oxide (NO) and xenon (Xe). These gases let us work out three things. The first was how to convert arrival time into electron kinetic energy (eKE), the energy the electron has once it has escaped. The second was the energy resolution, which was about 1% of the electron's energy (ΔE/E ∼ 1%). The third was how well the spectrometer collects electrons of different energies.

We wanted the vacuum level to be the same everywhere in the interaction region. To do this, we coated the liquid-jet nozzle, the skimmer, the gas nozzle and the magnet with colloidal graphite, a very fine soot. However, during our measurements, water molecules stuck to the graphite. This slowly changed the work function of the surfaces around the interaction region. The work function is the energy needed to pull an electron out of a surface. This effect, together with the streaming potential caused by electrokinetic charging inside the nozzle, can create a difference in electric potential across the interaction region.

To check for this, we measured the shift in the electron kinetic energy of the Xe photoelectron spectra. We did this for different distances between the liquid jet and the interaction point, before each measurement. We then adjusted the NaOH concentration and the flow rate of the jet to make the vacuum level even throughout the interaction region. We repeated the same measurement at the end of each set of liquid-jet measurements. The shifts in the vacuum level were smaller than our experimental error (Figure S1).

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) studies show that the chromophore hardly clumps together in the 5 mM solutions. They do suggest, however, that some hydrolysis takes place, meaning the chromophore reacts with water and breaks apart (Figures S2 and S3).

### Computer Calculations

We first worked out the ground-state geometry of the solvated chromophore anion, meaning the most comfortable arrangement of its atoms in water. For this, we used a multistep hybrid QM/EFP/MD approach that we developed earlier. It combines three tools. Quantum mechanics (QM) calculates the electrons of a small group of atoms. Effective fragment potential (EFP) treats the surrounding water molecules as a simplified model. Molecular dynamics (MD) follows how atoms move over time.

The system had three layers. The central QM region held pCE– and the five water molecules closest to the chromophore. An inner region of about 1000 water molecules was optimized under a QM/EFP description. An outer shell of water was relaxed using MD simulations with classical TIP3P force field parameters, a standard set of rules for how water molecules interact (Figure S4). We treated the QM part at the PBE0/(aug)-cc-pVDZ level of theory. This is a particular choice of mathematical method and basis set for calculating electrons. We added diffuse functions, extra mathematical terms that let electrons spread out, only on the oxygen atoms. We varied the radius of the water sphere around the solute from 10 to 36 Å. (An ångström, Å, is one ten-billionth of a metre.)

We calculated the first vertical detachment energy as the energy difference between the S0 and D0 states. S0 is the ground state, and D0 is the state the molecule has after losing one electron. We did this at the PBE0/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP level of theory, for a series of model systems that grew larger, up to about 10,600 water molecules. All water molecules except those in the QM part were treated as EFPs.

A structure with about 7,700 water molecules (R = 34 Å) gave a D0 vertical detachment energy that had settled to a stable value (Figure S4). We used this structure for higher-level calculations of the D0, D2 and D3 (π–1) vertical detachment energies. These calculations used the XMCQDPT2/SA(10)-CASSCF(12,12)/(aug)-cc-pVDZ+/EFP method. To mimic an electron leaving the molecule, we placed a very diffuse function outside the water sphere. We included it in the pure π valence active space, the set of electrons that can be excited.

We calculated the D1 (n–1) vertical detachment energy as the D0 vertical detachment energy plus the D0 → D1 vertical excitation energy (VEE). The vertical excitation energy is the energy needed to lift an electron to a higher state without letting the molecule change shape. For these excited-state calculations, we used a smaller system made only of QM and EFP.

We calculated the vertical excitation energies of the solvated neutral radical, the molecule after it has lost one electron, at the XMCQDPT2/SA(7)-CASSCF(11,11)/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP level. Here we used a mixed n/π active space, which includes both kinds of electrons. For the solvated anion, we calculated the vertical excitation energies with both the pure and the mixed active spaces. We used the XMCQDPT2/SA(7)-CASSCF(12,11)/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP and XMCQDPT2/SA(7)-CASSCF(14,12)/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP levels of theory, respectively. We used the Firefly software package for all electronic structure calculations. We ran the MD simulations with the NAMD software.
parts.results:
## Results and Discussion

### How the Chromophore Absorbs Ultraviolet and Visible Light

Figure 1 shows how strongly pCE– in water absorbs ultraviolet and visible light. We used a solution with 50 μM of pCE–. (A micromolar, μM, is a measure of how much of a substance is dissolved in a liquid.) We measured the absorption in 4 mm cuvettes, which are small clear containers. We then took the difference between two measurements: the absorption of 50 μM pCE– in 2.0 mM sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution, and the absorption of the 2.0 mM NaOH solution alone. (A millimolar, mM, is a thousand times more concentrated than a micromolar.)

The solution absorbs most strongly at a wavelength of 351.5 nm, which is an energy of 3.53 eV. This is a blue shift, meaning a move toward shorter wavelengths and higher energies. It is lower than the absorption maximum of the chromophore inside the protein (446 nm, 2.78 eV) and lower than the maximum of the chromophore in a vacuum (430 nm, 2.88 eV). The comb marks the first four vertical excitation energies of pCE– in water. A vertical excitation energy is the energy needed to lift an electron to a higher energy level without the molecule changing shape. We calculated these with our computer method, XMCQDPT2/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP.

### Vertical and Adiabatic Detachment Energies

Figure 2 shows the photoelectron spectra of pCE– in water. A photoelectron spectrum is a graph of how many electrons come out with each energy. We recorded it with three photon energies: 180 eV (a, d), 40.81 eV (b, e) and 3.02 eV (c, f). The spectra are plotted as nhν − eKE. Here, hν is the energy of one photon, eKE is the kinetic energy of the electron, and n is the number of photons. It equals 1 in panels a, b, d and e, and 3 in panels c and f.

The X-ray and EUV spectra in panels a and b are difference spectra. We subtracted the signal from the water itself from the signal from the whole solution. We then scaled the intensities so that the largest peak of liquid water's 1b1 valence band lines up with the largest peak of the solution. The 1b1 valence band is a group of electrons in water that are held fairly loosely.

To get the 180 eV difference spectrum, we fitted the recorded solution and water spectra with a sum of Gaussians. A Gaussian is a smooth, bell-shaped curve. Each curve stands for one source of electrons: electrons knocked out of pCE–, or electrons knocked out of liquid water and of water vapor. We fixed the widths of the water peaks, and the relative positions of their centers, to values from recent accurate measurements of liquid water's valence band. We set the energy scale by matching the water 1b1 electron binding energy to the accurate value reported in that same study. Subtracting the water peaks from the measured spectrum gave the difference spectrum in panel a.

For the 40.81 eV difference spectrum, we subtracted a spectrum of 50 mM sodium chloride (NaCl) from the pCE– spectrum. We first smoothed the NaCl spectrum with a 12-point quadratic Savitzky-Golay filter, a standard way of smoothing out random noise. We recorded these EUV spectra with a voltage of −25 V applied to the jet.

We set the energy scale of the difference spectrum in two steps. First, we used the low-energy cutoff, the point where electrons have zero kinetic energy, to calibrate a complete EUV reference spectrum. Second, we lined up a spectrum recorded over a smaller range of detachment energies, 5–11 eV. That spectrum has a stronger signal compared with its noise, so it is easier to read. We lined it up using the position of the largest water 1b1 peak.

**Figure 2.** (a, d) X-ray photoelectron spectrum of 5 mM pCE–, recorded with a photon energy of 180 eV. (b, e) EUV photoelectron spectrum of 5 mM pCE–, recorded with a photon energy of 40.81 eV. (c, f) Multiphoton UV photoelectron spectrum of 50 μM pCE–, recorded with a photon energy of 3.02 eV (410 nm). The X-ray and EUV spectra are scaled to the largest peak of liquid water's 1b1 valence band. The UV spectra are scaled to the largest photoelectron signal. (d–f) Straight-line fits (black) to the rising edges of the photoelectron signals (red) and the noise baselines (purple), on a logarithmic scale. We used these fits to estimate the adiabatic detachment energies (ADEs). (g) The arrangement of electrons in the first few energy states of pCE– in water, and in the matching neutral radical, calculated with XMCQDPT2/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP. Vertical excitation energies (VEEs) and vertical detachment energies (VDEs) marked with an asterisk were calculated with a mixed n/π active space. The rest were calculated with a pure π active space. The horizontal black and red lines labeled with numbers show the π and n orbitals, respectively, and show how many electrons occupy each one in each state. Arrows show the likely ways electrons can be knocked out, based on the arrangement of electrons in the states involved.

We fitted the X-ray difference spectrum of 5 mM pCE– with three Gaussians below 9.35 eV (Figure 2a). Above this high electron binding energy cutoff, the difference spectrum is mostly noise. Figure S8 shows how the centers of the Gaussians shift when we change this cutoff. From the fitted, subtracted data, we report the first two vertical detachment energies of pCE– as 6.76 ± 0.13 eV and 7.78 ± 0.13 eV. The lowest of these is very similar to the value for the chromophore of the green fluorescent protein in water. The position of the red Gaussian depends on the high cutoff, so we report it as 8.8 ± 0.2 eV to reflect this.

In the EUV spectrum of 5 mM pCE–, the electrons have kinetic energies above 15 eV. This means the signal from the valence electrons is essentially free from distortion caused by inelastic electron scattering, where electrons lose energy by bumping into other molecules. We fitted the difference spectrum with four Gaussians. When we let the fit be completely free, the two lowest-energy Gaussians had the same electron binding energy (about 7.7 eV) but very different widths. Their full widths at half maximum (fwhm) were 2 and 0.2 eV. These widths do not match the usual values for organic substances dissolved in water.

So we constrained the fit so that the width of the lowest-energy peak could be at most 1 eV. This gave the first three peaks electron binding energies of 6.9 ± 0.2, 7.7 ± 0.1 and 8.8 ± 0.1 eV. These agree with the values from the subtracted X-ray data. The EUV spectrum also has a peak at 9.8 eV that does not appear in the X-ray spectrum, and we cannot assign it. One possible explanation is that it comes from overlapping contributions from OH– (vertical detachment energy 9.2 eV) or from higher vertical detachment energies of pCE–.

Table 1 sums up the central vertical detachment energies from the X-ray and EUV spectra. They agree well with the values from our computer calculations. When we use a pure π valence active space, the calculated vertical detachment energies for the D2 (8.5 eV) and D3 (8.7 eV) channels differ by only 0.2 eV. So we expect the matching experimental bands to overlap, which makes it hard to say for certain whether a peak belongs to D2 or D3.

**Table 1.** Lower-energy vertical detachment energies (VDEs) of pCE– in water, together with the matching adiabatic detachment energies (ADEs), measured by X-ray, EUV and multiphoton UV liquid-microjet photoelectron spectroscopy (LJ-PES). The table also lists the vertical detachment energies calculated with XMCQDPT2/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP.

| Technique | hν (eV) | S0–D0 VDE | S0–D0 ADE | S0–D1 VDE | S0–D2/D3 VDE |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| X-ray LJ-PES | 180 | 6.76 ± 0.13 | 5.9 | 7.78 ± 0.13 | 8.8 ± 0.2 |
| EUV LJ-PES | 40.81 | 6.9 ± 0.2 | 5.8 | 7.7 ± 0.1 | 8.8 ± 0.1 |
| UV LJ-PES | 3.02 | – | 5.9 | – | – |
| Calculated | – | 6.7 | – | 7.8 | 8.5/8.7 |

a All values are in eV.

We can also find vertical ionization energies and vertical detachment energies using UV laser pulses that last only femtoseconds (a femtosecond is a millionth of a billionth of a second). To do this, we record photoelectron spectra with wavelengths that do not match any excited state. pCE– in water absorbs a lot of light at wavelengths below 400 nm. So, to avoid this resonance, knocking out an electron with several photons needs three photons. However, pCE– also absorbs light at wavelengths just above 200 nm (Figure 1). As a result, two-photon resonances make it impossible to use nonresonant multiphoton detachment photoelectron spectroscopy for pCE–.

Figure 2c shows the UV photoelectron spectrum of 50 μM pCE– recorded with 410 nm light. The pCE– concentration in these measurements is 100 times lower than in the X-ray and EUV experiments. Even so, the signal-to-noise ratio is excellent, meaning the signal stands out clearly from the noise. This is because there is no photoelectron signal from water: knocking an electron out of water would need four photons at 410 nm. The multiphoton detachment spectra are also fairly narrow.

We used our spectral retrieval software, LJscatter, to model how electrons with kinetic energies below 5 eV scatter inelastically. We also used a concentration depth profile for pCE–, which shows how its concentration changes with depth in the jet. We worked out this profile with molecular dynamics simulations, computer simulations of how molecules move (Figure S9). We then fitted two Gaussians to the spectrum. This gave values of 3hν − eKE of 7.3 ± 0.1 eV and 8.0 ± 0.1 eV. These values are higher than the one-photon vertical detachment energies from the X-ray and EUV spectra, so we do not include them in Table 1. However, such resonant multiphoton detachment measurements tell us about the vertical detachment energies of excited electronic states, and we discuss this in detail below.

Photoelectron spectra can also give a rough estimate of the adiabatic detachment energy. We find the electron binding energy at the point where the photoelectron signal begins to rise. A common way to do this is to fit a straight line to the rising edge of the signal and to the noise baseline, on a logarithmic scale.

Figure 2d–f shows this procedure for the X-ray (180 eV), EUV (40.81 eV) and UV (3.02 eV) photoelectron spectra of pCE–. The signal and noise baselines are shown in red and purple, and the points where they cross are marked with black circles. The adiabatic detachment energies from the three spectra (Table 1) agree with one another, at about 5.8 eV. This value is effectively the threshold for knocking an electron out, rather than a "true" adiabatic detachment energy.

This analysis assumes that, when an electron is knocked out, the molecule's equilibrium shape and the surrounding water change only a little. In that case, the Franck–Condon profile, the pattern of how likely different final shapes are, reaches the equilibrium shape of the neutral radical in water. We also note that hot transitions, which involve the molecule's vibrations, dominate the start of the photoelectron band, and they depend on temperature. The similarity between the UV, X-ray and EUV measurements suggests that all three methods can be used to estimate adiabatic detachment energies from the ground electronic state.

### Knocking Out Electrons at Resonant Wavelengths

To understand the resonant multiphoton photoelectron spectra of pCE– in water, we need to know its electronic structure. We calculated the first four vertical excitation energies and vertical detachment energies of pCE– in water with XMCQDPT2/(aug)-cc-pVDZ/EFP (Figure 2g). As a first approximation, we can use Koopmans' theorem to judge which one-photon routes are likely. Koopmans' theorem links the energy needed to remove an electron to the energy of the orbitals it comes from.

For example, the arrangement of electrons in Figure 2g shows that the ground state, S0, is likely to lose an electron and become D0, D1, D2 or D3. The first excited state, S1, is likely to become D0 or D3, and the second excited state, S2, is likely to become D1.

We now turn to the multiphoton UV photoelectron measurements. Figure 3 shows multiphoton photoelectron spectra of pCE– recorded with wavelengths between 410 nm (3.02 eV) and 310 nm (4.00 eV). These wavelengths reach the first two excited states (Figure 2g), which lose electrons to become D0 (vertical detachment energy about 6.7 eV), D1 (about 7.8 eV) and D3 (about 8.8 eV). We fitted the spectra with distorted Gaussians using LJscatter. We fitted the 400 nm spectrum with two Gaussians, the 380, 365 and 350 nm spectra with three, and the 310 nm spectrum with one.

The 310 nm spectrum also has a small contribution on the high kinetic energy side of the main peak, shown enlarged 20 times in Figure 3e. This roughly matches the red and orange peaks in the other spectra. But these features are so weak in this spectrum that fitting them is unreliable. The higher-energy red and orange peaks appear in all spectra. The lower-energy blue peak, however, does not appear at all in the 410 and 400 nm spectra. It first appears in the 380 nm spectrum, and its contribution grows as the wavelength gets shorter, until it dominates the spectrum at 310 nm (4 eV). This suggests that it comes from a detachment process near the escape point.

To learn what is happening when we use resonant wavelengths, we looked at how the photoelectron spectrum of pCE– depends on the power and wavelength of the laser pulses. Figure 4a is a log–log plot of peak area against laser pulse energy, for the three features in the 350 nm photoelectron spectrum of pCE–. On a log–log plot, a straight line with slope 1 means the peak area doubles when the pulse energy doubles. We found the peak areas by fitting three Gaussian kinetic energy distributions. We fixed their peak centers and widths to match those from the 350 nm spectrum in Figure 3.

Fitting straight lines to the data in Figure 4a gave slopes of 1.61 ± 0.06, 2.71 ± 0.09 and 2.61 ± 0.07. This suggests that the low kinetic energy peak comes from a two-photon process, and the two higher kinetic energy peaks come from three-photon processes. The slopes are not whole numbers because the electrons are knocked out through resonances, and the chances of absorbing light and of losing an electron are different. This fits what we see in Figure 3. The 400 nm spectrum is dominated by resonance-enhanced detachment through S1 with three photons, because resonance-enhanced detachment through S1 with two photons is not possible at that energy. As the wavelength gets shorter, the competing two-photon process starts to appear at very low kinetic energy. Its share of the spectrum grows as the wavelength shortens, until it eventually dominates the spectrum recorded at 310 nm.

The two higher kinetic energy peaks come from three-photon resonance-enhanced detachment. So plotting their central kinetic energy against photon energy can tell us a lot about the two-photon detachment process. Figure 4b shows this plot. The peak centers from Figure 3 are shown as empty circles. The peak centers from the 410 nm spectrum in Figure 3 and from extra measurements (Figure S10) are shown as filled circles. The central kinetic energy of the red peak stays roughly the same for photon energies below about 3.6 eV. The central kinetic energy of the orange peak, however, rises twice as fast as the photon energy rises.

The red peak's kinetic energy stays the same as the photon energy changes. This is a sign of a three-photon resonance inside the range of energies where electrons can escape freely, from which electrons escape indirectly. Its value, a kinetic energy of about 1.2 eV, is the energy gap between the three-photon resonance S m and the neutral radical D k that results (Figure 4c).

We can explain this behavior with Franck–Condon factors, which describe how likely a molecule is to end up in each final shape. A molecule vibrates in many ways, called normal modes. If the equilibrium shape changes only a little along all of these modes between S m and D k, then the 0–0 transition, where the molecule stays in its lowest vibration, remains the strongest. This is what we expect for biological chromophores when an electron leaves through a shape resonance. Also, if the higher vibration levels are not much populated when the molecule is excited to S m, then the 0–0, 1–1 and 2–2 transitions from S m to D k all have similar maximum strengths. This gives the same electron kinetic energy no matter what the excitation energy is. We discuss this Franck–Condon analysis in detail in our earlier work.

In the gas phase, negatively charged molecules that do not change shape much when they lose an electron tend to keep their vibrational energy. This was seen for isolated pCE– using anion photoelectron spectroscopy. It will also be seen for pCE– in solution if the surrounding water relaxes more slowly than the multiphoton detachment process lasts, which is about 300 fs. The trend in the kinetic energy of the orange peaks supports this (Figure 4b). The vibrational energy gained when the molecule is excited to S1 is kept when the electron leaves. The measured electron binding energy of S1 (2hν − eKE) does not depend on photon energy (Figure S12), and its average value is 4.1 ± 0.1 eV. The matching 3hν − eKE values range from 7.2 to 7.8 eV (Figure S12). The UV photon energy is less than the vertical electron binding energy of S1, but more than the threshold for detachment. So the process that produces the orange peaks can be thought of as above-threshold ionization.

If there were no resonances at the two-photon level, the average electron binding energy of S1 would be the difference between the D0 vertical detachment energy and the adiabatic excitation energy (AEE) of S1:

(1) VDE − AEE ≈ 2hν − eKE

The adiabatic excitation energy is roughly the average of the absorption and emission maxima (Figures 1 and S9). Putting AEE of about 3.1 eV and 2hν − eKE of 4.1 eV into equation 1 gives a vertical detachment energy of about 7.2 eV. This is 0.4 eV higher than the value from our X-ray measurements. The difference can be explained by how well the two routes overlap with D0: two-photon detachment from S1, and one-photon detachment directly from S0. The higher vertical detachment energy for two-photon detachment from S1 fits with the orange peaks in the UV photoelectron spectra getting wider. Their widths range from 0.8 to 1.5 eV for the 400–350 nm spectra, compared with 0.7 eV for the lowest-energy peak in the X-ray spectrum.

We now turn to the blue peak in the UV photoelectron spectra of pCE–. Its kinetic energy is about 0 eV in most spectra, so we can only get an accurate value from the 310 nm data (Figure 3e). This gives hν − eKE = 3.4 ± 0.1 eV. We also recorded a two-color photoelectron spectrum, exciting the molecule to S1 with 350 nm light and then knocking out an electron with 266.7 nm light (Figure S11). It gives hν − eKE = 3.7 ± 0.1 eV, which is 0.3 eV higher than the value from the 310 nm spectrum. We put this difference down to competing detachment processes from S1 and S2.

The S2 absorption band shows up as a small shoulder around 310 nm in Figure 1, and it has no matching peak in the fluorescence spectrum (Figure S13). The S2 state has nπ* character, meaning its electron sits in a different kind of orbital from the π orbitals. The calculated oscillator strength of the S0–S2 transition, a measure of how strongly a transition absorbs light, is near zero. But the state can still gain intensity through vibronic coupling, where vibrations and electronic states mix.

There is experimental evidence that the nπ* state is populated. In ethylene glycol and dimethylformamide solutions, the absorption band shifts less with the solvent than in water. Also, the fluorescence anisotropy, which measures how strongly the emitted light keeps the direction of the absorbed light, drops quickly when the excitation wavelength is shorter than about 320 nm. Based on Koopmans' correlations (Figure 2g), we expect detachment from S2 to produce the neutral radical in its first excited state, D1. The drop in hν − eKE between the 350 and 310 nm spectra could then come from signals from these two routes overlapping, with the S2–D1 vertical detachment energy being lower than the S1–D0 vertical detachment energy. Moreover, for one-photon detachment, equation 1 becomes VDE − AEE ≈ hν − eKE. This gives a vertical detachment energy of about 6.8 eV, the same as the value from our X-ray measurements.

The red and orange peaks in the 335 nm spectrum (Figure 3), which come from detachment from S1, do not follow the trend seen at wavelengths longer than 350 nm. Also, the one-photon electron binding energy of the blue peak from the two-color spectrum after excitation at 350 nm (3.7 ± 0.1 eV) is about 0.4 eV smaller than the average two-photon electron binding energy of the orange peak (4.1 ± 0.1 eV). This is true even though both come from S1–D0 detachment.

The change in trend might come from a switch between two-photon S1–D0 detachment above 335 nm and one-photon S1–D0 detachment at 335 nm. This is because hν + AEE = 6.8 eV, which is just enough to knock an electron out of S1 with one photon. However, transient absorption experiments on pCE– and PYP in solution have reported that solvated electrons form when the molecule absorbs two pump photons. This process was identified because the solvated electron signal grows with the square of the exciting laser's pulse energy. Since both pCE– and PYP absorb light in an excited state near the S0–S1 absorption maximum, these measurements suggested that solvated electrons come from a high-lying state near the range of energies where electrons can escape freely.

In our photoelectron measurements, exciting the molecule to this state could give a different overlap with D0. That would affect how much vibrational energy is kept when the electron leaves, and so the kinetic energy we see. As a result, the three-photon detachment to D0 could happen step by step. First, the molecule is excited to S1. Then it is excited further to a high-lying state near the range of energies where electrons can escape freely. Finally, an electron is knocked out to form D0.
